speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is not merely another technological trend.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is reshaping industries, transforming organisational modes and models and redefining the skills needed to create value.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the transformation is evident across sectors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Firms are accelerating AI adoption and workers are seeking opportunities to reskill and adapt.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This underscores a critical point, that technological progress, if unsupported by structured education and training strategies, risks widening capability gaps rather than closing them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To build a workforce capable of harnessing AI, AI literacy must be embedded across the entire learning life cycle, from the early years of schooling to continuing education and training (CET) for working adults.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: AI literacy does not begin with sophisticated tools or computer programmes or complex algorithms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It begins much earlier, with students developing the ability to understand how systems work, recognise the limitations of automated output and exercise independent judgement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a world where generative AI can produce essays, code and analysis within seconds, the differentiator will not be access to technology.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will be the capacity to engage with these tools critically and to harness them to enhance meaningful work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As AI tools become increasingly embedded in everyday life, foundational competencies must be sequenced more deliberately.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A student's ability to interrogate an AI system at graduation depends on habits of reasoning formed years earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the primary level, this means cultivating cognitive discipline – recognising patterns, following logical sequences, distinguishing correlation from causation and interpreting simple data.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They form the mental scaffolding required to understand how automated systems arrive at decisions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But Sir, as students mature, abstraction and systems thinking can be introduced deliberately at the secondary level.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Learners can examine how algorithms are designed, how datasets shape outputs and how human choices influence technological outcomes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And by pre-university, students should be capable of critical interrogation – evaluating AI-generated content, identifying limitations and weighing ethical trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This sequence reflects not only curricular design but developmental readiness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, what we are talking about here is the scaffolding of AI learning, a scaffolding of AI education throughout the entire learning journey in schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore should ensure that its approach is equally progressive, inclusive and systematic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this roadmap in place, the next challenge is how schools teach and assess in an AI-pervasive environment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education in an AI age should not overload students with content but rethink pedagogy to emphasise reasoning, judgement and creativity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, these are competencies that AI cannot replicate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Teachers should position AI as a tool to deepen learning, not as a shortcut.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lessons and projects could encourage students to question outputs, iterate solutions and critically evaluate information.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If AI tools are used in assignments, evaluation should thus measure meaningful application of concepts, the reasoning behind solutions and thought processes, rather than merely the final product.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Practical approaches could include reflective journals documenting AI use, oral defences to explain reasoning and process documentation, such as prompt logs or iterative drafts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Project-based assessments requiring real-time collaboration and problem-solving can further reveal student understanding and agency.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Transparency, accountability and authentic demonstration of skills should guide assessment design rather than prohibit or limit AI use.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Equally important, Sir, is cultivating skills AI cannot replicate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Leadership, empathy, ethical judgement, collaboration, public speaking and resilience remain essential to holistic education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Teachers play an indispensable role in developing these capacities, ensuring students grow intellectually, socially and emotionally into confident, capable individuals.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education must remain about shaping thoughtful, adaptable citizens, not merely producing technically competent operators.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The success of an AI-ready curriculum depends on teachers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even the best-designed lessons and assessments fall short if educators lack confidence in using AI tools, integrating them into learning or guiding responsible, ethical use.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Teachers in AI-augmented environments must act as facilitators, mentors and guides.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And continuous professional development should track emerging AI trends to keep educators equipped.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And now, Sir, something on inclusive AI education for different learners' profile.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Tailored programmes and scaffolds are essential to ensure all learners can fully engage with AI learning environments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Adaptive learning systems can personalise content to a student's pace, proficiency and cognitive profile, providing targeted support to address gaps and reinforce strengths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Inclusion also depends on structured support within schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Educators and learning specialists should be trained to use AI tools in ways to complement individual learning profiles.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, analytics dashboards to identify early signs of struggle, designing customised practice pathways or integrating AI-assisted feedback to support self-paced learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The aim is not simply to adopt AI because it is available but to use it thoughtfully to respond to the diversity of learners in our classrooms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By embedding inclusive design principles in AI education, from platform design to classroom practice, we can ensure technology lifts all learners, not just those already advantaged.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Inclusive AI education strengthens equity and affirms our commitment to leaving no student behind.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think AI can be used, Sir, to really create learning environments in the hardware and the very structure of the classrooms to enhance how the classroom functions, to complement the ability of teachers to deliver in the classrooms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had mentioned earlier, Sir, that core to our education experience, are our teachers, and may they always remain core, our physical teachers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How we can explore AI to perhaps enhance what a teacher is doing, create teacher avatars or one educator in the classroom, for example, that that person could be doing multiple things at the same time in different parts of the classroom.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, this might sound like something from science fiction, but I believe that it is possible, Sir, to have a version, say, of a teacher Jeffrey in the classroom and then perhaps create AI avatars of teacher Jeffrey that could perhaps go and work in different groups in the classrooms concurrently and then come back again where teacher Jeffrey talks, say, to the rest of the classroom.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would also address the issue of class sizes indirectly in a way.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have talked about class sizes and reducing class sizes for quite some time now over the past five, 10, even 15 years since I came into Parliament.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And what we are talking about in class sizes is not so much reducing the class size per se but improving the ratio of the teacher and the student in the education experience.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, if you have a class size of 20, one teacher is a ratio of 1:20.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You can either reduce the class size to 10 or perhaps have two teachers come in.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You have the same effect therefore of 1:10 ratio.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us explore how we can perhaps use AI in a way that would be able to address the issue of class sizes in a creative manner, such that the end goal is not simply reducing the class size to smaller numbers in a class but enhancing and improving the teacher-student ratio.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the school classrooms, a robust AI education ecosystem requires infrastructure and support mechanisms to enable learning across life stages.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While schools lay the foundation, working professionals must access structured pathways to upskill and remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would complement existing offerings from polytechnics and universities, such as Professional and Adult Continuing Education academies, which already provide professional courses in AI and data analytics.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, artificial intelligence is reshaping the skills, work and society our young people will inherit.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Since its inception in 1984, the GEP has played a crucial role in nurturing some of our most academically able students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Many alumni have gone on to contribute meaningfully across academia, Public Service and industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The programme was, in many ways, a product of its time, a deliberate effort to ensure that academic excellence was not left to chance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The centralised model, which extracted students from their schools into smaller number of designated centres, inevitably reduced social mixing at a formative age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Whether or not elitism was intended, the programme also came to be perceived as accessible only to the affluent, especially with an increasing correlation between socio-economic status and academic results.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: If implemented thoughtfully, this approach has the potential to stretch our brightest learners while strengthening, rather than fragmenting, our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Such a design transforms these schools, many of which are located in heartland neighbourhoods, into local "centres of excellence", enabling students to stretch their abilities in environments that are both familiar, yet socially diverse.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Beyond academic growth, this approach exposes learners to peers from different socio-economic backgrounds, fostering empathy, resilience and social awareness, qualities as critical to a child's development as intellectual development and growth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: At the same time, neighbourhood schools can cultivate distinctive programmes and reputations for nurturing talent, creating a distributed ecosystem of excellence that benefits students, educators and the broader community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As such, I hope that thoughtful alignment of module locations and timetabling with students will ensure the programme remains accessible and manageable without placing undue strain on students, parents or caregivers, in terms of travelling from school to the centre.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The placement and operation of these centres is not merely administrative.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Instead, they should broaden and deepen engagement with subjects in ways the standard curriculum cannot, fostering curiosity, creativity and applied thinking.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: They should thus provide guided opportunities for students to apply their skills in meaningful contexts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: For example, students in advanced English modules could explore literature, journalism or creative writing, extending well beyond what is assessed in schools or national examinations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mathematics modules might introduce basic financial literacy, logic puzzles, or problem-solving in everyday contexts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Science modules could offer hands-on experimentation, design-thinking challenges, or introductory environmental and sustainability projects suitable for nine- to 12-year-olds.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: To complement these experiences, enrichment modules could include informal mentorship opportunities with educators, researchers, or even industry professionals who can guide students' exploration in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), the arts, or humanities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: While not formalised as a teaching approach, these interactions allow students to gain early insight into real-world applications of knowledge, nurturing responsibility, resilience and ethical awareness alongside intellectual growth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: By situating enrichment within neighbourhood schools, broadening the scope of learning beyond examinations and nurturing pathways for high-potential students, we can combine academic excellence with inclusivity and social cohesion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is significantly larger than the average in advanced industrialised countries where the numbers are 21 and 23 respectively and speak to the disparity that still exists in the amount attention our kids from their teachers in our public schools, relative to other countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this is not an argument that smaller class sizes automatically translate into superior outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That evidence is, indeed, mixed, although there is indication that the greatest benefits do come in the early grades and when egregiously large classes of 40 are moderated into something closer to 30.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, that is far stronger evidence that smaller class sizes improve things like classroom management, strengthen student learning and reduces teacher's stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is eminently commonsensical and is one that is already abundantly clear when one actually speaks to teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notably, the Ministry has also considered that smaller class sizes have clear benefits in certain specific circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, in recognition of the challenges faced by the young learners adapting to a new educational setting, Primary 1 and 2 classes are kept at 30 students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Children in the former GEP, who may require more customised learning to fully unlock their intellectual potential, enjoy classrooms of closer to 20-plus, and foundation classes, which focus on building fundamentals for students who require additional support, range between 10 and 20 students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I argue that the benefits of smaller classrooms should not just be limited to these special cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, the most recent edition of the Teaching and Learning International Survey points to another clear problem with large classes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Paradoxically, these added hours come at the expense of classroom hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Allied Educators in teaching and learning would be scaled back.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is the opposite direction of where we should be heading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, it is clear that the debate is not so much about whether we should reduce our class sizes, but about how.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The straightforward solution is, of course, to hire more teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Ministry standard response to this has been that this will compromise the quality of the teachers that we hire while robbing other sectors of talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOE also says that there is a dearth of teaching talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have always found such arguments to be disingenuous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, are we implicitly suggesting that teachers from two decades ago, where there were more of them as a share of the workforce, were somehow not of the same quality as teachers today, or the investments in our future workforce are somehow a lower priority than those that drive our economy today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a sense, economics also tells us the solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Should we worry about the ability to attract talent into teaching?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should pay our teachers more or reduce their workload.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will solve the chicken and egg problem of teachers who otherwise wish to remain in the profession but leave due to burnout.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As any human resources professional knows, retention is more than half the battle compared to recruitment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if we believe that the transition to smaller class sizes will take time, there is a more immediate solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can reduce the effective size by adding a teaching aid or Teaching Assistant for every classroom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such Teaching Assistants can guide students that lag behind during breakout sessions or handle disruptive students so that the teacher can carry on with the curriculum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another upshot of such professionals is that they can also take on administrative and planning tasks or at the very least, do so in collaboration with the main teacher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This burden is clearly something that teachers struggle with, as it occupies the majority of their time, distracts them from what they were primarily hired to do and adds unduly to their stress levels.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: MOE's move from T-scores to achievement levels was thoughtful and reduced fine differentiation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But when families still believe that performance at age 12, Primary 6, influences access to certain secondary schools and future pathways, they will still invest more time, more effort and money to secure an advantage.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When stakes are concentrated, pressure and spending concentrate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That is the dynamic of an arms race.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When DSA becomes another prized gateway, families respond with earlier coaching and curated portfolios.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We now risk running two races, an academic race through PSLE and a portfolio race through DSA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In an AI-disrupted world, careers will shift multiple times and skill upgrading must be continuous over life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: AI tools can now personalise practice and provide instant feedback.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But many advanced tools are subscription-based or require strong home support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If unmanaged, AI becomes the new tuition and the arms race becomes digital.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some argue that as long as employers value academic credentials, then competition is inevitable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But labour market norms will not shift overnight.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In an AI-driven world, success will depend less on early sorting and more on adaptability, deep thinking and lifelong learning habits.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These cannot be built in a sprint to age 12.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, make AI a national equaliser – guarantee baseline access in schools, teach AI literacy, and shift assessments toward reasoning and authentic application.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Under such a pilot, standards remain aligned with national expectations, students graduate with recognised qualifications such as the GCE, mobility and transfer options are preserved, and subject-based banding can start at an earlier age and deploy teachers according to the needs of the students using a “flexible class size” model instead of a “universal small class size” model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Not small classes everywhere, but right-sized classes, flexible and fit for purpose.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Evaluation should examine academic performance, student well-being, tuition reliance and socio-economic mobility.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Scaling should be considered if outcomes are at least as strong, with reduced pressure.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But there is urgency in building an education system ready for a very different future, one centered on lifelong learning, adaptability and strong character.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Dismantling the PSLE, DSA and AI-driven arms race is only the beginning of redesigning education for the long race ahead.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, during the recent Lunar New Year, my soon-to-be 11-year-old cousin Denise asked me a question I could not answer.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She asked, "Why does the PSLE have to exist?" Before I could respond, Denise clarified herself. "I'm not saying no exams.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But why does how I perform on a single day determine the outcome of my six years in primary school?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If AI can do so many things, why do I still need to memorise so many things for PSLE?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why can't we just add up the scores of all of my weighted assessments?" My response was, why indeed?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What struck me the most was not the stress that Denise had described, one and a half years away from sitting the PSLE.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was a decision that she had already made on her own.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Going into Primary 5, she had pre-emptively dropped Higher Chinese, not because she had done badly but because she was worried she could not cope in Primary 6.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She had looked at the road ahead, thought about her korkor and jiejie's experiences and decided to limit herself before a single PSLE paper had been sat.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I had no good answer for Denise, I promised her that I would raise this in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What Denise had identified intuitively is a tension that sits at the heart of our education system.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our desired outcomes of education for our children to become confident persons, self-directed learners, active contributors and concerned citizens.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By the end of primary school, we want our students to know their strengths and areas for growth.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet we assess six years of learning via a high stakes, timed, written examination across four subjects in a week.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We say one thing and we measure another.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a new observation, but it has never been more urgent.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We just passed a Budget that commits billions to AI adoption that urges Singaporeans to move up the value chain, to exercise judgement, creativity and human insight.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet come September, will we be assessing the 35,000 12-year-olds who will sit the PSLE on any of these skills?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the long overdue review of our education system.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should have an education system where the default is that every child passes through compulsory education without a high stakes written exam determining their trajectory at age 12.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question is not whether to assess, but how.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Removing PSLE as a default would free up months of curriculum time currently consumed by PSLE exam preparation and give our students more time and space to develop genuine strengths, deeper interest in subjects and also 21st Century Core Competencies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Denise did not ask us to make school easier, she just asked for it to make sense.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Yet in Singapore, once every six years, parents face intense pressure over two milestones: Primary 1 registration and the PSLE.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The uncertainty of school placements, combined with the high stakes of academic outcomes, creates enormous stress – stress that no parent should face alone.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Primary 1 registration process focuses on what the parents have done.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Whether they live nearby, are alumni, or volunteer.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I have deep respect for their efforts to do what they believe is best for their children.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But we must reflect on how or whether the system unintentionally amplifies anxiety, undermines fairness and detracts from the schooling experience.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As MOE embarks on a review of the Primary 1 registration process, I have two points to make.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In our meritocratic society, every child who works hard should have the opportunity to thrive.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can the process better support students of diverse backgrounds and talents?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This build on calls by my hon friend, Sengkang Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, regarding the benefits of later start time for adolescent health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The stakes are equally high for our primary school students.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Between ages seven and 12, a child's brain and body are in a state of rapid fundamental construction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Science tells us that deep sleep stage, non-Rapid Eye Movement sleep is when the pituitary gland releases the vast majority of growth hormones necessary for physical development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For these younger children, getting the recommended 10 hours of sleep is not a luxury.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is a biological requirement for physical health and cognitive wiring.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When a primary school student is chronically under slept, the first thing to suffer is executive function, the ability to manage emotions, follow instructions and focus.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We see this manifesting in classrooms as increased irritability and the lack of resilience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By failing to protect their sleep, we are effectively handicapping their formative years, trading long-term neurological health for short-term academic grind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For adolescents, this is a matter of biology.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: During puberty, the brain undergoes a phase delay.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Their bodies do not release melatonin until much later.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It has been said that waking a teen at 6.00 am is physiologically equivalent to waking an adult at 3.00 am.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While MOE has brought forward personal learning device default sleep modes to 10.30 pm, we must also address wake times.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By incorporating co-curricular activities (CCAs), structured work instead of homework and remedials into these hours, we ensure that when a child reaches home, school responsibilities are largely complete, making the lights out boundary more achievable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Rather than relying on school level autonomy, we need a clear national standard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let us set the bell for 8.30 am and give our children the rest they need to reach their full potential.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Trade is the lifeblood of Singapore, making it essential for us to facilitate as much trade as possible.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This requires a focus on establishing numerous companies and fostering a mindset of entrepreneurship that can create significant impact.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Nurturing this entrepreneurial mindset and skill set should begin at a young age and schools are the perfect environment for this exposure.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: By integrating entrepreneurship into the CCAs, students can learn about business establishment and experience what it means to be an entrepreneur.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: There are already some schools implementing this but we should make this apply across all schools for students to be given the opportunity to participate.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This co-curricular activity can be one of many programmes launched in primary and secondary schools.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Trade associations and chambers can play a vital role in developing the curriculum and nurturing young entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: By implementing such a curriculum, students will acquire a diverse range of skills, including marketing, distribution, operations, finance, resourcefulness and negotiation.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Introducing entrepreneurship in schools will activate their innovative and creative minds, positioning us as a nation of creators and innovators capable of establishing companies and business solutions.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In time, this initiative will not only increase the number of companies but also enhance our global trade presence, connecting Singapore with other regions of the world.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He listed measures, cool paint, faster fans, physical education (PE) attire, mixed mode air conditioning for halls.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If an unfair learning gap is forming, can we afford to wait?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Every MOE school is already air-conditioned: computer labs, science labs, libraries, lecture theatres, staff rooms, admin offices, all air-conditioned.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry is now installing mixed mode air-conditioning in school halls, so the electrical infrastructure is there.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The only rooms without air-conditioning are the classrooms where 420,000 children spend most of the day.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should extend aircon to the rooms that matter most.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A primary school teacher told me by 11.00 am in the morning, classrooms are unbearably hot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fans just circulate hot air and create noise that drowns out teaching.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They ask to go to the toilet just to escape the heat.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Teachers cannot teach effectively in that heat either.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To avoid thermal inequality, we should set one.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2023, the Government's Mercury Taskforce designated community centres and sports halls as airconditioned cooling spaces for the public.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But for schools, reduce outdoor activities, relax dress code, send children home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we will air-condition community centres for adults, but close schools for the kids.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: International schools and independent schools have air-conditioned classrooms.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The children who can least afford the learning penalty are paying it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On running costs, 130 schools already have rooftop solar under Solar Nova.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Expand it to all schools and offset the additional electricity partially.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am not asking to switch on air-conditioning all day.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Set a target temperature, switch on when the thermostat exceeds it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MOE headquarters (HQ) already runs a similar system, centralised air-conditioning with automatic start times and cut-offs.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I rise to speak on inter-faith learning for social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is the result of deliberate policies and hard work, by our founding fathers over many decades, that build trust across the communities.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I would describe this as the Singapore model of practical harmony – not just tolerance, but day-to-day cooperation, a shared civic space and the instinct to navigate differences thoughtfully in our society.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In a multiracial, multi-religion society, this harmony must be renewed in every generation.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, schools are where this renewal can be made real.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Inter-faith learning should not be treated as a niche topic or something left to certain communities, certain neighbourhoods or only to those who are already exposed.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we want mutual understanding to become a shared national norm, every student should have balanced, age-appropriate exposure to major religions and beliefs that shape Singapore in a way that builds trust, reduces stereotypes and equips them to navigate difference with confidence.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I therefore hope MOE can consider deepening inter-faith education in three practical ways.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, MOE can strengthen a clear structured baseline of inter-faith literacy with age-appropriate content that focuses on understanding, common values and how Singapore manages diversity.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The aim is civic understanding and mutual respect for the various religions in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, MOE can make inter-faith learning more experiential.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Schools can be supported to run structured dialogues, visits and interfaith learning journeys.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Here, MOE can partner and work with non-Government organisations, for example, Inter-Religious Organisations, which has a long and extensive experience in engaging different faith communities in a constructive and practical way.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, MOE can support teachers and school teachers with ready-to-use resources and facilitation guides.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I believe many educators will welcome clearer frameworks, case studies and training so that they can facilitate confidently, especially when sensitive questions are being raised.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, my point is that ultimately, inter-faith understanding is not about preventing conflict, it is about building social capital.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is about ensuring that our young grow up with the instinct to ask, to listen and to respect.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: When students learn early that different faiths can coexist and share the same space, we strengthen the roots of cohesion that hold Singapore together.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we want Singapore to remain united in a more polarised world, we must invest not only in academic outcomes, but also in the social fabric.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Inter-faith learning is one of the quiet, high-impact investments that will pay dividends for decades to come.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This poses a risk to their physical well-being and cognitive development.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Primary schools provide two to 2.5 hours of PE weekly, but logistics can eat into this short duration.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is insufficient to build a robust physical foundation in children, who need at least 60 minutes of moderate to rigorous physical activity daily.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Improving fundamental motor skills early enhances movement confidence, cultivates lifelong habits and broadens our pipeline for national athletes and combat-fit soldiers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Better physical fitness also improves academic performance and cognitive focus.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For a small nation, our competitive edge lies in the quality and resilience of our human capital.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Not all PE time needs to be conducted by PE professionals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Subject-based teachers could conduct movement-based lessons where science concepts, like velocity, can be taught through active outdoor experimentation, bringing knowledge to life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By raising the floor of our children's fitness, we can raise the ceiling of what Singapore can achieve.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Students should be not just learners or users of AI, but innovators and creators of AI.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: AI-ducation – the use of AI to personalise learning, identify gaps and guide teaching – can help students progress at their own pace while freeing teachers from repetitive tasks to focus on mentorship and meaningful learning.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: To be AI-ready, how will students and teachers be equipped with the resources and skills needed to thrive in an AI-ducation environment?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Our next bound of staff development must focus decisively on AI proficiency.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: First, AI can be a force multiplier to address staff strength challenges.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: We need to up the AI proficiency of all staff so they can free up "human bandwidth" for high-value student interactions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Second, teachers must be practitioners of AI before they can be teachers of AI.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Beyond standard professional development, is there a structured AI proficiency roadmap so every teacher can use AI confidently as a daily assistant?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: How do we ensure AI tools are deployed to subtract admin workload rather than add a new layer of tech management duties?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Is there a framework to regularly benchmark teachers' AI competency?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Our students and educators must not just use AI.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: They must innovate it, create it and lead its future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We know the outcomes are unequal, yet we lack the granular data needed to design truly effective interventions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We track economic indicators monthly, yet assess educational equity only when politically convenient.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Annual tracking would reveal whether our interventions are working or merely well-intentioned.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, data linking income and ethnicity in university access would answer a critical question: Are financial barriers or other factors driving the gap?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: MENDAKI subsidy data would show whether lower-income Malay students are accessing higher education at improving rates.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Without this, we cannot distinguish between solvable financial constraints and deeper systemic issues.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, dropout rates by income and ethnicity would identify where students are falling through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Malay community deserves policies built on evidence, not presumption.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has the technical capacity for this level of analysis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: MOE has taken important steps to use AI to reduce administrative workload for teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But if we stop there, we risk using a transformational technology merely to improve efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: First, AI must be used as a pedagogical tool, not merely as an efficiency tool.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond automation, how might we use AI to redesign pedagogy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It allows students to progress at different paces and receive targeted support without stigma.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Used thoughtfully, AI can shift assessment from ranking students against one another to tracking their individual growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: MOE has also rightly spoken about reducing the arms race in education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: AI could help us further rebalance the system, retaining necessary standards while placing greater emphasis on calibration and support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If such formative systems can be scaled up, we may have an opportunity to rethink the timing and role of high-stakes examinations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Research suggests that very early high-stakes selection does not necessarily improve long-term outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, it narrows learning and intensifies anxiety without improving standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, if continuous diagnostic assessment can provide clearer signals of student progress and learning gaps, then early high-stakes exams may not need to carry such disproportionate weight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Relatedly, how does MOE evaluate whether early high-stakes selection meaningfully improves long-term student outcomes compared with delaying such assessments until students are older?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Second, as AI replaces more routine cognitive work, we must strengthen distinctly human capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As structured cognitive tasks become automated, our advantage will lie increasingly in the human capabilities like imagination, collaboration, resilience, physical vitality and initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In the AI era, these will become even more central.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: How are these competencies being embedded in classroom practice and assessment, and not just articulated in policy documents?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Ensuring space for the arts, sport, recreation, project-based learning and entrepreneurial exploration will be critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In an AI-driven economy, how does MOE ensure that these areas are protected and strengthened within the curriculum?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Reducing the arms race is not about lowering standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is about aligning our standards with the capabilities that matter most for the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Third, we should address concentrated demand for certain primary schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Persistent pressure around Primary 1 registration suggests that demand remains concentrated in a number of highly sought-after schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, what key factors determine whether a successful school model can be replicated elsewhere?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, talent pathways must reflect long-term development, not early acceleration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we seek to reduce excessive academic pressure, we must also ensure that competitive intensity is not simply directed to other domains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The original intent of DSA was to recognise diverse talents beyond academics in sports, the arts and other areas of strength.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: However, in a competitive environment, DSA may inadvertently incentivise earlier and more intensive specialisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, this increases the risk of burn-out, injury or loss of intrinsic motivation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, in this context, could MOE consider conducting longitudinal studies to evaluate whether DSA supports: (a) a sustainable national talent pipeline in the respective domains, and (b) reducing both short-term and long-term outcomes for individual students?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: AI is shaping the way we learn and the way we work.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it also raises deeper questions about judgement, equity and the preservation of human creativity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our students are already encountering AI tools in their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: AI literacy must mean more than technical familiarity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It must include the ability to question outputs, detect bias, understand limitations and exercise ethical judgement.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A student should know not only how to generate an answer through AI, but how to interrogate it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In practical classroom terms, this may mean requiring students to produce an initial draft before consulting AI and assessing them on how they evaluate and refine AI suggestions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It may mean presenting students with an AI-generated essay and asking them to critique its weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Mathematics and Science, we might place greater weight on explaining reasoning rather than simplify and presenting a solution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the arts, AI, of course, can generate various variations, but the creative direction must remain firmly in the hands of the student.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: AI should be a thinking partner, not an answer engine.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It should expand imagination and not standardise it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It should accelerate our ability to iterate but not eliminate intellectual struggle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must be careful that creativity is not stifled by convenience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The most complex processing tool ever is the human brain.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would be deeply ironic if, in building ever more powerful machines, we allowed our own capacity for deep thinking and problem solving to weaken.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some degree of cognitive effort, even friction, is necessary for growth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If AI removes that effort entirely, the learning becomes hollow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, we must ensure that there is equitable access.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the conversation does not end at graduation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Continuous learning is becoming essential not only for engineers, programmers, accountants, designers, logistics consultants and frontline supervisors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Training should be directly linked to real workplace tasks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And smaller firms that lack in-house capacity will need further support.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lower-wage workers must not be left behind as automation advances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It should not be a niche advantage enjoyed by a small group, but a common capability that strengthens our collective resilience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whether it empowers or diminishes us depends on the norms and structures we build around it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we are intentional, we can raise a generation that masters AI without being mastered by it and a workforce that uses AI to enhance judgement rather than outsource it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In doing so, we ensure that technology amplifies what is makes us uniquely human.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Chairman, our young graduates are entering the workforce at a time in a disrupted age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI is becoming more advanced, even at entry-level tasks.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And throughout their careers, they will need to adapt and pivot several times, as the pace of change and skills obsolescence increases.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: If our education system does not evolve, there will be a growing mismatch between graduates' skills, job expectations and experiences and evolving market needs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our education system, especially our IHLs, must become more agile and proactive in anticipating future skills demands, especially in this AI disrupted age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This must happen at every level and not just at our universities, but in our polytechnics and ITEs too.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, in my maiden speech at the debate on the President's Address, I said that SkillsFuture risks is becoming a supermarket of choices, plenty of choice but no clear ladder to climb towards better career outcomes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I want to return to that concern and ask the Ministry to take three concrete steps.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A three or four-year bachelor's degree cannot keep pace with that kind of velocity, and neither can our current continuous education ecosystem that is still struggling to get employers to recognise lifelong learning credentials at all.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, it functions largely as a digital filing cabinet.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the new AI programmes our IHLs have been launching.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore prides itself on being open to the world and our upskilling framework should be no different.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a vast ecosystem online of world-class universities offering Masters level micro-credentials through various platforms.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister has made AI a centrepiece of this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world not waiting, our workers are not waiting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a university educator and administrator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As I follow the recent discourse on AI and education both in Singapore and globally, I observe two seemingly polarised views on the impact of AI on education, particularly higher education and CET.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: One is that little will change and the other is that everything must change in the age of AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I see elements of truth in both views.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: On the one hand, AI will affect both content – what is taught – and instructional methods – how knowledge is shared and learnt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Students will need to know how to use AI tools and interpret AI output with discernment, as many Members have raised, while new technologies can enable more personalised learning experiences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, there is genuine concern about cognitive offloading if students rely excessively on AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This underscores that there is no substitute for building foundational skills in thinking and writing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is a need for clarity on what should change and what should be retained in regard to education in the AI age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: What is becoming clear is that tertiary education, in particular, needs to be revamped more quickly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: When students can acquire knowledge for themselves with the help of AI tutors that are available around the clock, IHLs need to consider what value they can bring to their students and hence, how to make the best use of curriculum time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It should no longer be about lecturers downloading information to students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Time spent in classes would be more productively used for case discussions, problem-solving and Socratic dialogue with facilitators and peers, to maximise opportunities for mutual learning, evaluation and reflection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: IHLs are also uniquely positioned to help students develop interpersonal skills, make friends and build networks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: To their credit, our IHLs are already alert to the needs in this changed environment and are feeling their way forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Various pilots are being done to revamp curriculum and update instructional methods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is also clear that AI will significantly influence how student learning is assessed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: If instructors assign take-home essays, I think it would be unrealistic to ask or expect students not to use AI tools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Trying to police unauthorised AI use could lead to contentious disputes between faculty and students in all but the most clear-cut cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: With different forms of assessment, there is also a need to better reflect the range of knowledge and skills that students acquire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A single course grade may not fully capture a student's competencies and skills particularly when there are both technical concepts and skills to master, as well as an evaluative or problem-solving dimension.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Students are expected to master economics, accountancy and business concepts, apply these to business decisions through case discussions and collaborate effectively in teams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A single course grade or Grade Point Average offers limited insight into these distinct dimensions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It may therefore be useful for an academic transcript to reflect multiple components, knowledge and technical skills, evaluative and applied capabilities and interpersonal competencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While the first component may be more objective, the latter two are arguably more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The University of Michigan has piloted skills transcripts for engineering students to highlight teamwork, problem-solving and technical proficiencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Stanford University Integrative Learning Portfolio Lab helps students create digital portfolios that capture academic, co-curricular and personal experiences beyond traditional grades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry elaborate on what is doing to encourage or support innovation in learning assessment, whether there is ongoing research in this area and what can be done facilitate systematic sharing of good practices and learning points across institutions?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, when I speak with students and working adults, the question is rarely about the number of courses available.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is this: "If I invest time and effort in learning, will it genuinely move me forward?" In Singapore, we have long believed that effort should open doors, that hard work, not background, determines opportunity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That belief is central to our social compact.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Support must feel integrated across skills acquisition, job transitions and progression.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A fragmented journey erodes confidence; a coherent one strengthens it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lifelong learning must translate into real mobility, not just participation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not enough to move someone into a job quickly if that job does not reflect their upgraded capability.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When effort visibly leads to advancement, confidence strengthens naturally.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, a clear framework should be set for policy decisions.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A single agency simplifies the journey for the learner, jobseeker and worker.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in resource-constrained segments, should employment-driven outcomes or longer-term career development training needs take priority?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lifelong learning succeeds only when employers signal that skills are recognised in promotion, pay and job redesign.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If retraining does not shift progression pathways, workers will hesitate, regardless of subsidies.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a changing economy, every Singaporean who is willing to adapt should be able to see a clear path forward.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If implemented well, this reform will strengthen trust in upward mobility for the next generation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Chairman, I support MOE's continued efforts to strengthen SkillsFuture as a pillar of lifelong learning, especially as our workforce navigates rapid shifts in technology and industry demand.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As of today, we have a wide and growing menu of courses and subsidies under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But for many Singaporeans, the hardest step is always the first step, knowing what course I should choose, whether this course aligns to my interests, my aptitude and also my longer-term aspirations.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, the reality is this: those with stronger networks will have a higher likelihood of knowing people working in emerging or high-value industries.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They can talk to these people to ask about what kind of skills they should acquire, what kind of course they should take so that they can enter such industries.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But the truth is those without networks or social capital, however, have to spend more time, more energy, more resources figuring out which pathways to take.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Surely, our system can do better to reduce such costs, so that decisions can be made better.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I call this SkillsFuture "Taster Sessions", at lower costs or no cost. "Taster Session" itself gives a flavour of what industry is like or what skillsets you require.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A good "Taster Session", however, should provide answers to basic questions, such as "What is this course about?", "What are the skills required for me to do well in this industry or sector?" Furthermore, such Taster sessions can also provide a broad roadmap, a landscape of professional pathways.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What are the positions that are there in this industries, and what kind of skills I should acquire, so that I can assume responsibility in these roles. "Taster Sessions" can also cover clear learning pathways.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In the event that a learner is interested to deep dive, these pathways should be grouped in a way that is easily understood by individuals, grouped by job role, skills type, level of difficulty or industry type.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we are able to do this well, individuals will have information and better understanding of the stakes involved before committing time, energy, money and even, potentially, a career change.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially important for emerging and specialised areas, where interest is high, but understanding is often lacking.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Whether be it frontal technologies, green capabilities or strategical domains, what we want is for every Singaporean to be able to enter this fields with eyes wide open.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Chairman, providing "Taster Sessions" can further strengthen equity, given how those with weaker networks and lower social capital often have limited means to understand the scope of course and industries.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To summarise my cut, SkillsFuture "Taster Sessions" can help to close the information gap and enable individuals to make better decisions, because do we not make many decisions every single day?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, I support the Government's strong investment in AI skills for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That is a genuine achievement and the result of deliberate, sustained policy work over decades.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The question is not whether we have done well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The question is whether we are developing the full range of human capacity for the future economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies the fastest-growing skill categories for the coming decade.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They span across two domains, analytical reasoning and creative thinking on the cognitive side, empathy, social influence and self-awareness on the affective side.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Both are identified as co-equal drivers of the future workforce value.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our current system has invested heavily in the cognitive mode, that is analytical, convergent and precisely measurable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences framework identifies that at least eight distinct cognitive systems – linguistics, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalist.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A system that assesses primarily through linguistic and logical-mathematical channels is measuring only a subset of human potential, not its full range.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Researchers Mayer, Salovey and Caruso, established that emotional intelligence, comprising of self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and relational skill, can be measured and developed.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Their model for emotional quotient (EQ) showed that performance and leadership outcomes are comparable to, and in some domains exceed, those of cognitive intelligence quotient (IQ).

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Research by Mary Helen Immordino-Yang and Antonio Damasio demonstrated that emotion and cognition are neurologically integrated.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The prefrontal cortex, responsible for executive function and higher-order reasoning does not operate independently of the limbic system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is biologically impossible to build memories, engage complex thoughts or make meaningful decisions without emotion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Affective disengagement impairs the cognitive performance even when the analytical capacity is intact.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is significantly above the OECD average of 66%.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Research establishes that it actively constrains cognitive flexibility and creative risk-taking.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Researcher Barker and colleagues examined the daily activity logs of 70 six-year-old children against standardised measures of executive function.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Their finding was direct, the more time children spent in less-structured, self-directed activities, the stronger their executive function scores are.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Executive function, goal pursuit and cognitive flexibility is precisely what the AI-era economy will value.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Executive function develops through the experience of self-direction.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Developing the full cognitive and affective spectrum is not supplementary to academic rigour.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is the condition under which academic rigour produces its maximum return.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Students register a project or hobby each semester, and schools provide the infrastructure, such as makerspaces and music rooms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The rationale draws from the research at the Stanford Center on Adolescence, found that young people who develop personal purpose through self-directed exploration demonstrate greater academic motivation, stronger mental health outcomes and more robust career trajectories than those whose goals are externally assigned.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The difference between consultation and co-governance is consequential.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In co-governance, the participant is present for trade-offs, constraints and decisions where competing priorities cannot all be satisfied.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That particular experience is where affective intelligence develops in practice.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Researchers Zeldin, Camino and Mook examined youth-adult governance partnerships across multiple institutional settings and established that genuine partnerships, involving real decision-making authority, produce durable improvements in youth self-efficacy, empathy and civic belonging.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The effect was significantly stronger in conditions of genuine co-governance than in consultative arrangements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The proposal to form Student Policy Committees, with school leaders being the facilitator and advisors to the committee.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This will provide genuine standing in discussions on student welfare, facility use and sustainability goals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Students are briefed on the constraints, the budget, the logistics and their input carries formal weight.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Rotation between different groups of students, distributes the developmental benefit broadly rather than concentrating it among a narrow student cohort.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Researcher Erik Erikson, in "Identity, Youth and Crisis", identified the age 15 to 25 as the critical psychosocial window for identity formation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Subsequent neuroscientific research also confirms that adolescence represents a period of heightened neuroplasticity, specifically in areas in governing self-concept, risk evaluation and social cognition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We should do more to invest before the age of 25.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: After this window, neuroplasticity would have largely closed for the most consequential function.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In 1959, the British physicist and novelist CP Snow delivered a lecture at Cambridge, which was later published as "The Two Cultures".

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That intellectual life had split into two mutually uncomprehending groups: the scientists and the humanists, who had largely stopped understanding or respecting what the other did.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Between them sat a gulf of mutual contempt that was quietly crippling society's capacity to solve its most serious national problems.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What Snow identified at the civilisation level, we can observe in our daily classrooms, boardrooms, teams, community and everyday life today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The analytically formidable student who cannot read a room and the relationally gifted student whom our assessment architecture cannot see.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Two intelligences sitting side by side, but neither recognising the other as intelligence at all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They will naturally yield to the consensus of their group and disregard the richer connective and effective diversity of others.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Stone's warning was that societies which allow this bifurcation to harden do not merely lose cultural richness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The challenges that matter most requires both cognitive and effective domains in genuine integration.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That is true in 1959, it is truer today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must continue to sharpen ourselves, respect capabilities of our connective and affective diversity, and make better decisions for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, as Deputy Chairperson of the Education GPC, my colleagues and I remain fully committed to ensuring Singaporeans have access to education at every stage of life, including pathways beyond the conventional routes we have long accepted.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As our nation intensifies efforts in AI education and promotes lifelong learning, we must ensure the right infrastructure supports every keen learner, regardless of their starting point.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is about building futures, not just acquiring knowledge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I urge a comprehensive review of capacity to ensure no qualified student is left on the sidelines.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As one of the Members of Parliament for Marsiling-Yew Tee Group Representation Constituency (GRC), I have previously raised in this House the proposal for a new ITE in the North.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This could double as a dedicated lifelong training centre to serve the growing population in the region.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It could partner closely with Republic Polytechnic for a seamless "through-train" programme, allowing smooth progression from foundational to advanced skills.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It could also collaborate with corporates in the nearby JTC industrial areas, enabling learners to apply skills directly on the job, secure employment upon graduation, or return easily for upskilling.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
