text: Such a facility would enhance access to practical, skills-based education, bridge gaps, and foster a stronger culture of continuous growth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need holistic programmes to reach those who might otherwise fall through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore call for deeper collaboration with initiatives such as the YMCA's Vocational and Soft Skills Programme, which equips out-of-school youth and youths-at-risk with job competencies and vocational skills to rebuild their confidence.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of those young children feel lost due to negative peer influences or challenging family backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Normalising and expanding such programmes align closely with the Prime Minister's vision: every Singaporean, regardless of starting point, deserves a fair chance to pursue their aspirations and realise their full potential.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is an investment in our people's talents, ensuring no dream is deferred due to financial barriers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   To support the implementation of the SkillsFuture initiative, the People's Association (PA) has been offering SkillsFuture@PA courses at various Community Clubs (CCs) since 2016.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This programme has been in place for nearly 10 years now.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To encourage more Singaporeans to utilise their SkillsFuture training credits, I hope that SkillsFuture@PA programme can be further expanded.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition to CCs, it could also extend to running courses at the Residents' Network Centres.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would provide greater convenience and companionship for seniors and those with mobility issues, motivating them to sign up and participate. : Chairman, educating Singaporeans develops our only natural resource – our people.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By expanding capacity, building targeted facilities, partnering with industries and community programmes, and reforming finances, we can make lifelong learning the norm, not the exception.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us commit to this today, for the sake of our youths, our workers, our nation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The ITE today is a launchpad for many young Singaporeans to build meaningful careers.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The next phase, however, is not only access but progression across a lifetime.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If lifelong learning is to work, progression must be legible.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I think of one Singaporean I know, Mr Abu Bakar Siddiq, who started out in the Normal (Academic) stream, went on to ITE, polytechnic to pursue engineering, and then went to work, got sponsored for his degree and has now completed his masters.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: His story shows that your starting point does not determine the finishing line and that progress must be open.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we strengthen this pathway, I have three questions for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, can the Minister update how MOE will give greater formal weight to workplace proven competencies with assessments that are rigorous and recognised across employers?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, will the Minister consider piloting a structured conditional university pathway for top performing ITE and work study learners anchored on sustained workplace achievement and continued upgrading without implying that university is the only outcome?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, a future ready education system is not one that sorts students early, but one that keeps doors open throughout life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If every pathway can lead forward, more Singaporeans will keep going further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: I declare my interest as the senior executive of an educational institute that trains and certifies adult educators for SkillsFuture courses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: The lifelong learning ecosystem in Singapore has transformed over the past 11 years since the launch of the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: The efforts of SkillsFuture Singapore and its partners have made training and reskilling affordable, accessible and of high quality, catering to the diverse needs of learners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Adult educators are critical to the quality of CET, just as our school teachers ensure the quality of education in our schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: At the Budget debate last year, I recall the hon Member Mr Xie Yao Quan spoke about the importance of the professional development and recognition of adult educators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: This public registry will support the professional development of adult educators and boost confidence in our CET system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Beyond setting minimum standards, we must also encourage and recognise excellence within the adult educator profession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: The Institute for Adult Learning, where I am from, will be inducting more Adult Education Fellows, recognising them as leading educators in their respective fields who can inspire other adult educators and share their expertise with the professional community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: This would put adult educators, as the custodians of lifelong learning, on par with the teaching profession in terms of recognition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: In this era of rapidly changing job and skills requirements, adult educators play a key role in motivating and inspiring adult learners to keep learning and acquiring new skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Adult educators need to innovate in their teaching and facilitation methods, based on the latest research in adult learning, and using AI and new digital tools where appropriate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: They have to be exemplars of adult learning themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: I believe that as we rebalance our focus between pre-employment training and CET, it is timely to strengthen our recognition of adult educators.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You can take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Chairman, I want to speak about affiliation and the balance that MOE must strike between school identity, diverse learning needs and fairness.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The mechanism of school affiliation and parents' alumni affiliation has been long part of our education landscape.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They help to sustain school ethos, community, and also tradition.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many alumni continue to contribute meaningfully back to schools and this spirit should be preserved.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But in today's context, MOE should also assess whether affiliation now might have resulted in unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Does it confer disproportionate advantage to some, weakened perception of fairness, meritocracy and social mixing?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One practical issue is how large cut-off points gap linked to affiliation can translate into different academic readiness in a classroom, and this makes targeted teaching harder and increase preparation burden on teachers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The cut-off point between an affiliated student and a non-affiliated Primary 6 can be very large.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is not an isolated case, because several schools have similar wide affiliation related cut-off points gaps.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This matters, because in our current AL system, some bands cover a wide range of marks.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, AL 6 spans between 45 marks and 64 marks, and AL 5, 65 to 74 marks.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, a one point cut-off point difference can represent a large spread in terms of academic readiness, what more a 10-point gap?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This can significantly widen the range of learners' profile in the same subject classroom.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This will in turn cause increased differentiation demands and make classroom and curriculum planning more complex, even as we move to have implemented our full subject-based banding (FSBB).

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While FSBB helps with subject level grouping, it cannot remove the wide difference in readiness within a subject class.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A second issue is what affiliation incentives to upstream.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: See, large affiliation advantages can fuel unhealthy primary school chasing earlier.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A possible unintended consequence is families make primary school choice not really based on values, culture or programmes, but because they are trying to secure an easier affiliated school pathway for a good secondary school later.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Over time, this can amplify inequalities, because the ability to move house, arrange childcare, mobilise alumni connection is not evenly distributed among the population.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, I would encourage MOE to consider whether the current school affiliation mechanism for entry to secondary school needs to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Well, I have some suggestions in this regard.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To be clear, the goal here is not to abolish school identity, but to ensure that identity does not come at a cost of public confidence in fairness or unintentionally weakening social mixing.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This links to the Primary 1 admission as well, especially under Phase 2A, which gives priority to parents who are alumni of the school.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: MOE has to balance legitimate community ties with the principle that schools should remain inclusive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Chairman, I appreciate MOE's effort to broaden pathways and enable our students to make better career choices, such as having educational career counsellors in our schools.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is important because it helps our students and also our young adults to decide what to pursue.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I think more can be done with regard to this, so that we can see large and more meaningful change, especially for those who have fewer networks.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This cut is with regard to internship, externship, learning journeys and structured career exposure.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, many of these opportunities exist, but access is uneven.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In a recent Clementi community run, I spoke to a student who shared with me that his school very soon, about in one week's time, they will have a sabbatical week for secondary four cohort.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These students can choose from a range of different programmes to gain exposure beyond classroom.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And he also shared with me his senior, Year Five, previously, just did an internship during school breaks.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, as a former educator, I understand his worldview, but I also know this is not true for most of our secondary schools in Singapore.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, structured exposure if done well, becomes an equaliser, because it substitutes for who you know and it helps students to build confidence, aspirations and a clearer sense of fit.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, I urge MOE to consider these three moves.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The aim is to ensure the experiences do not sit within some schools, but they are made available throughout our system, especially our non-IP schools and less resourced educational institution.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We can work with industry partners and school leaders to curate such experiences.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such experiences should not be one off but should be a sustained exposure that helps students to understand what the nature of the work is like, what kind of skills is required, what pathways exist.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we believe in equity, we must design a first access for students who have fewer resources or come from disadvantaged background.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should remove practical barriers in this regard.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And beyond SkillsFuture course, we should also scale this at adults as well for short learning journeys for adults.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This will give our adults a more realistic view.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Chairman, resilience should not depend on which school a child attends.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In some schools, resilience skills, peer systems and early detection are embedded.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In others, they depend heavily on local bandwidth and priorities.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If resilience is foundational, certain elements must be guaranteed nationally.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Finland embeds well-being as a formal objective in its national curriculum.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Denmark mandates a weekly class, Klassens Tid, dedicated to emotional dialogue and conflict resolution.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Japan's Tokkatsu, part of its national curriculum, systematically develops social responsibility and emotional regulation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The principle is clear: centralise standards and accountability, decentralise delivery and innovation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Denmark uses national digital well-being audits to systematically track student mood and welfare trends.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Finland's three-tiered support model ensures timely intervention for students who need more help.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our Charter should define timelines for counsellor access, minimum training and supervision standards for peer supporters, structured referral pathways.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Accreditation should be tiered and developmental, recognising capability-building rather than compliance.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The Charter aligns these under clear national guardrails.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: International evidence shows resilience improves when it is embedded, measured and systematised.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: With structured standards, every student receives consistent support regardless of school.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: The Minister has outlined efforts to support disadvantaged students, nurture human-centric qualities in the age of AI and refresh the CCE curriculum.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: In 2023, the Singapore Symphony Orchestra brought 200 students to a concert.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: Half had never attended one; a third lived in rental or smaller flats.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: If one shared arts experience can do this, imagine what sustained engagement could achieve for bullying prevention, socio-emotional development and social mixing.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: The arts also engage kinesthetic learners, foster creativity and strengthen problem-solving.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: This is not about adding to teachers' burdens but equipping them with trained partners.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: I saw this firsthand at a Playback Theatre session by the Singapore Drama Educators Association, where audience members share real experiences of bullying and trained facilitators play them back through improvised performance.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: The practitioners proposed this as an avenue to address bullying by building empathy and supporting restorative approaches.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: As Singaporean artist Tan Swie Hian said, "Art is not just a reflection of life; it is a catalyst for change".

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: Our children are works of art themselves who can be powerful catalysts of change.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: By bringing the arts into education, we can help our students grow not just academically, but as empathetic, resilient and creative individuals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Big thanks to MOE, partner disability agencies and staff.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But the numbers being diagnosed and the demands are increasing and our support models must grow stronger.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: First, on mainstream schools, from access to consistent quality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Over the past decade, MOE has strengthened in-school capabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Primary schools now run structured programmes, such as School-based Dyslexia Remediation, Circle of Friends peer support, and the TRANsition Support for InTegration (TRANSIT) initiative.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But two areas need attention in the mainstream schools setting.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Parents still report differences in early identification, teacher confidence and consistency of support across schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: We need a clearer national tiered framework that defines what every classroom teacher must be able to do, what school-based specialists provide and what requires multi-disciplinary intervention including for mental wellness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Support should not depend on which school a child happens to enter.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For many SEN students in mainstream settings, academic access alone is not enough.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Executive functioning, self-advocacy, emotional regulation, work habits and digital responsibility and so on must be systematically embedded, not treated as optional add-ons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: These are foundational for lifelong learning and employability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Next on special schools, expanding the capacity and reimagining their purpose.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: On the SPED side, much more support had been put in.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: No young person should thrive for years in our SPED schools to face then a drop into uncertainty.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Like the hon Member Ms Denise Phua, I would like to applaud the Ministry's significant investments, over the past decade, in differentiated provision of support across the education system.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: This has enabled more students with SEN to access educational pathways suited to their profiles of needs.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Mainstream schools now provide students with SEN access to the national curriculum as well as with support in the form of teachers trained in SEN, SEN Officers, and from the multi-tiered system of support.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Within this context, students with SEN not only benefit from the challenge from access to the national curriculum but they also have the opportunity to learn alongside their peers.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Students with SEN thrive in mainstream environments when necessary supports are in place.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are some students with SEN who are able to engage with aspects of the national curriculum, but whose consistent participation in classroom instruction depends on supports that are not always available within the school environment.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: These may take the form of additional services targeting areas like learning, executive functions social skills, as well as emotional and behavioral regulation.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: When such support is not consistently available, the students' ability to participate in classroom instruction and progress within the national curriculum may become affected.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: This may impact, in the short term, engagement, learning and social interaction of such students.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: But it may also affect motivation and identity over time as well as potentially longer-term consequences on employability and participation within society.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Access to such supports may depend on availability, cost and coordination across settings, which can be within hospitals, social service agencies or private providers.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: In such circumstances, the responsibility for sustaining access to learning may shift from institutional arrangements within schools to the capacity of individual families to coordinate supports across educational, healthcare and social service settings.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: It is about how continuity of meaningful participation in mainstream schools is sustained for students with SEN with support needs that are not consistently available within the school environment.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Minister's clarification on this matter.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: Chairman, as inclusion deepens in our mainstream schools, we must ensure that support arrives early enough and scales quickly enough to ease pressure in the classroom.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: In Primary 1, teachers are not only teaching literacy and numeracy.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: They are helping children learn how to sit still, sustain attention, regulate impulses and transition between tasks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: When several students in one class struggle with these foundational skills, the teacher spends much of the lesson managing behaviour.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: MOE already conducts systematic screening for literacy and numeracy at Primary 1 and SEN officers support teachers in identifying social-behavioural difficulties.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: It allows schools to identify early on which cohorts may require heavier classroom support before strain accumulates.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: Importantly, this information could be linked to calibrated manpower deployment.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: Where a Primary 1 cohort shows higher-than-usual support needs, temporary para-educator or co-teaching support could be deployed earlier rather than after prolonged escalation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: And where support density within a class is particularly high, flexibility in class composition or size should be considered.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: What matters is whether the structure of the class matches the needs within it.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: When early intervention is effective, behavioural and learning gaps often narrow.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: Support intensity reduces as students mature and manpower can then be redeployed to incoming cohorts.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: In this way, we move from reactive escalation to early calibration.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: This approach lightens teacher workload, reduces cumulative strain across levels and ensures that children receive timely support during their most formative years.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: If we detect early and deploy early, we support our teachers, strengthen student outcomes and give parents confidence that inclusion remains both compassionate and workable.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: (In Mandarin):   Bilingualism is central to Singapore's identity, yet gaps remain.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: I speak from personal experience as a former Language Elective Programme (Chinese) student.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: I am proud to enjoy my mother yongue.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Bilingualism should not be a policy, it should be a skill students embrace with confidence and pride.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Yet mastering two languages is no easy feat.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: We need targeted support for weaker learners, stronger teacher training and curricula that make languages relevant and engaging.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Assessments should reward practical use, not just exam results.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying
text: Only then can bilingualism become a lifelong skill, empowering our students and sustaining our cultural heritage.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, bilingualism today cannot be sustained by schools alone.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: Languages weaken not when they are difficult to learn, but when they are no longer lived outside the classroom.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: If we want mother tongue proficiency to be sustained, we must continually enrich the language environment so that children here use and enjoy the language in everyday settings.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: This is why the next phase of bilingualism must be a whole-of-community effort.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: Because bilingualism is not only taught in schools, it is sustained in communities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, a cut on bilingualism will not be complete without me speaking in my mother tongue.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: In Tamil, please. :   Why do we refer to mother tongue as mother tongue?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: When we mention "mother", what we recall are love, support and nurturing.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: These beautiful feelings have to be refreshed in our hearts as we speak in our mother tongue.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: Therefore, we cannot teach mother tongue in schools alone.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak
text: Hence, let us come together and expound the motherliness of our mother tongue.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, as a small nation without natural resources or hinterland, Singapore's success has always depended on our people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Education has been a core engine that equips Singaporeans with what they need to take on new challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the post-Independence years when survival was priority, we focused on basic education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the 1970s, we shifted away from a one-size-fits-all approach and improved educational outcomes through streaming and differentiated pathways.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: From the late 1990s, we broadened our definition of success by recognising diverse strengths and abilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Since the 2010s, we have increased emphasis on students' holistic development and strengthened lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: During the Budget and Committee of Supply (COS) debates, Members spoke about the uncertainty and challenges brought about by the geopolitical paradigm shift, artificial intelligence (AI) and the existential threat of climate change, and proposed many ways to better prepare Singaporeans, through education, for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In our next bound of education reform, we want to support every Singaporean to learn and reach their full potential, regardless of their starting point, and to seize opportunities in a fast-changing world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In line with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's call for a "we first" society, we will "Learn For Life, Together".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, I will speak about how we will refresh our education system in three ways.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Students of different strengths and needs will be developed to their full potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will also uplift disadvantaged students and support those with Special Educational Needs (SEN).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To prepare students for the future, we will further strengthen our focus on holistic development, where students develop core values and critical life skills, and learn to interact and build bridges across differences, instead of just chasing after academic grades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will also encourage and equip our students to be innovative and enterprising, to pursue deep learning in an AI-transformed world and support them in their journey towards lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Lastly, let us work together, educators, parents as well as industry and community partners, to build a stronger education ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My colleagues will share in greater detail how we will achieve some of these efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Senior Minister of State David Neo will speak about creating a student-centric education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will explain how we support lifelong learning beyond schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Minister of State Jasmin Lau will share how we are preparing Singaporeans for an AI-transformed future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And Senior Parliamentary Secretary Syed Harun will set out our efforts supporting students with SEN and strengthening bilingualism.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our education system serves a broad spectrum of learners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Through Full Subject-Based Banding (Full SBB), students can build on their strengths in different subjects and learn at their own pace.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We stretch those with academic strengths and talents, while providing additional support to disadvantaged students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Over the years, we have made moves to customise education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Notably, Full SBB allows secondary school students to take subjects at different levels based on their strengths, interests and learning needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My colleague Senior Minister of State David Neo will provide more details later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is part of our broader effort to recognise and nurture the students' strengths as well as interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Darryl David and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked for smaller class sizes to better customise education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Denise Phua called for a flexible class size model, right-sized and fit for students' needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This proposal has been raised over the years by Members from both sides of the House.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We agree that having smaller class sizes can improve teaching and learning, as teachers can better cater to the learning needs of their students especially those who need more support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is precisely why we have smaller class sizes for students with greater needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We deploy more teachers and allied educators to support and scaffold their learning and channel more of our resources to help them learn.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In upper primary, foundation subjects are taught in smaller classes, which in most instances can be 10 to 20.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For the Learning Support Programme, its class sizes are of about eight to 10.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And in Full SBB, different subjects range between 20 and 40 students, based on students' learning needs and the nature of the subject.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are learning from our experience, over the last few years, with smaller class sizes for students with greater needs, and are studying how best to calibrate class size to bring about engaging and effective learning environments for our students, while managing teacher workload.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Assoc Prof Lim asked why we cannot simply hire more teachers to bring class sizes down.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But we would need to increase this much further to achieve across the board class size reductions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, we are contending with a tight labour market, especially for those we want to recruit as teachers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We need to select not just for those with qualifications, but also the aptitude to teach and the heart to nurture future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yet our local workforce growth is slowing and Singaporeans have many attractive career options in the public and private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also suggested hiring more allied educators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In expanding our allied educator pool, we are focused on the high priority, more specialised support functions that our schools and teachers need the most, such as school counsellors and SEN officers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They play important complementary roles alongside our teachers in supporting students of different strengths and needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To achieve this, with the limited manpower available, we have been progressively scaling back the deployment of allied educators in teaching and learning and helping them to transition into roles of greater need over the past nine years, through work attachments and training.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This was reported in the media in 2016, a Parliamentary Question by Nominated Member of Parliament Yip Pin Xiu in 2019, a Parliamentary Question by Member of Parliament Leon Perera in 2020 and a Parliamentary Question by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim in 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, contrary to the Member's claim, this was not a new shift announced in tandem with the increase in teacher recruitment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I thought to set the record straight to soothe the "sucker punch" that the Member said he felt and to make clear that the Ministry had not been disingenuous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Assoc Prof Lim also suggested that co-curricular activities (CCAs) and Learning Journeys are secondary to classroom instruction, and can thus be outsourced to free up teachers' time so that they can teach more academic classes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While MOE has indeed been bringing in more coaches, instructors and administrators to help relief teacher workload by running CCAs, let us be clear.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: CCAs are an important part of holistic development and our teachers' role in CCAs are not merely administrative.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They help nurture our students to develop critical social, emotional competencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, if we were to reduce class sizes by restructuring teachers' duties and ask them to teach more academic classes, we would need to weigh the possible impact on students' holistic development and teachers' overall working hours.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As you can see, the considerations underlying class sizes are not simple and straightforward.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Mr Darryl David and Ms Denise Phua can be assured that we are studying them carefully to better support our teachers and students in a sustainable way for the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Next, as announced in 2024, we will refresh how we support students with academic strengths and talents, and discontinue the Gifted Education Programme (GEP) in its current form.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are ready to share some of our implementation details.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, all primary schools already offer school-based programmes beyond the curriculum to stretch and challenge students who have strengths and talents in English, mathematics and science.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They have debate competitions and Excellence 2000 (E2K) math and science.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: On Ms Elysa Chen's queries, these students will be taught by trained educators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, almost all primary schools have at least five teachers trained to teach such students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Where needed, MOE will provide additional teacher resourcing to schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Teachers and school counsellors will also be given training, curriculum resources and professional development.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Through these, schools can better support their students, encouraging exploration, creativity and personal ownership of learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Students who can benefit from further stretch can choose to attend centre-based advanced modules after school, at a nearby school centre.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They will no longer need to leave their school and transfer to another school that hosts the GEP for daily learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, they will remain in their own schools and continue to learn with their friends.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Besides English, mathematics and science, there will be interdisciplinary modules inspired by real-world problems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To be clear, these modules are not intended to give students a leg up in examinations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Rather, they are designed to further cultivate curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Take, for example, the interdisciplinary module on "Playgrounds".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Students will explore them as community systems, integrating social studies, science and mathematics to tackle real world design challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They will study how to make such spaces safe, investigate the science of movement, and through empathy exercises, design inclusive playgrounds for diverse users.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Last year, we conducted a trial of these modules, which was well-received.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These schools have good geographical spread and are accessible via public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Schools can also identify students using additional resources of information, such as teacher observations and students' work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Rather than having a single entry point at Primary 4, students can also join at the end of each semester at Primary 4 and Primary 5, making this more porous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Next, let me speak about how we are helping students from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Education has helped spur social mobility in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We want our children to know that as long as they are prepared to put in effort, they can do well in life regardless of their starting point.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We would like to assure Mr David Hoe and Mr Abdul Muhaimin that MOE provides additional support for disadvantaged students in their education journey and that financial barriers will not impede their educational aspirations and progression.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In total, about 133,000 students will benefit annually.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, students from lower-income households can tap on the MOE Opportunity Fund for co-curricular activities, learning experiences and personal learning devices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr David Hoe will be glad to hear that we also have measures to support these students' aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, about 100 primary and secondary schools, with a higher proportion of students from lower-income households, receive additional resourcing for after-school programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These include mentoring, interest-based activities and learning journeys, which broaden students' perspectives and develop their aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Centennial Fund Award also supports polytechnics and ITE students from disadvantaged backgrounds by providing mentorship to guide them on their career and life goals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Sally, whose name has been changed to protect her privacy, is a Primary 6 student at Naval Base Primary School.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: She was anxious in school and lacked confidence in her studies because of her challenging home environment and her burden of having to care for her younger brother after school each day.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Sally's teachers encouraged her to join the school's Beacon for Life programme, which is an after-school programme supported by MOE, which offers academic support as well as activities that build teamwork, resilience and emotional well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The school also worked with community partners to customise support for Sally and Sally's family also received Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) ComCare and assistance from a Family Service Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The wraparound care and support given to Sally helped build her confidence in school and social interactions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, Sally participates actively during lessons and her CCA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Sally's journey illustrates what we can achieve when schools and communities collaborate closely to uplift our students and their families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: MOE will strengthen our support for disadvantaged students like Sally and schools' partnership with the community in support of ComLink+.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Existing initiatives, such as Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce (UPLIFT) Enhanced School Resourcing and Guiding and Empowering students for Affiliation and Resilience to Unlock their Potential, which respectively provide additional resourcing and school support, such as afterschool programmes, will be streamlined into one single support package, which we will further enhance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our schools will provide customised support to students, by strengthening partnerships with community stakeholders, such as self-help groups and others.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will also provide stronger and more timely wraparound support for students and their families by tightening coordination between schools and key agencies, such as Social Service Offices and Family Service Centres.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our goal is clear: we want every child in our schools to achieve his or her full potential, regardless of background.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But that would mean all of us have to work even more closely together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Next, we have made significant progress over the years in supporting students with moderate-to-severe SEN, who attend Special Education (SPED) schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This includes enhanced curriculum quality through a National SPED Curriculum; strengthening partnerships between General Education and SPED schools; and professionalising SPED educators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We thank families, social service agencies (SSAs) and other Government agencies, who partner us in the broader SPED ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Syed Harun will share more details later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our education system has long been recognised for its academic rigour and excellence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While these remain important, they have never been our only focus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As our world rapidly transforms, we do not want our students to simply be good at aceing exams today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We want them to be trailblazers for tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This calls for a reimagining of education – a reform and refresh of how we prepare our students to be resilient, well-rounded and thoughtful.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To achieve this, one challenge we must first confront honestly is the education arms race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many parents still regard the PSLE and Direct Schools Admissions (DSA) as measures of success, which is perfectly understandable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If we were to look deeper, these perceptions stem from the belief that getting into popular schools will help their children do well in life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The fixation on grades and achievements and the excessive competition it generates, draws us away from what really matters.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It diminishes the joy of learning, it takes time away from character building and it pits our children against one another.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We know it takes more than just academic grades to do well in life and in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Preparing for the future, especially one that is so uncertain, means anchoring our education system in holistic development.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Denise Phua, Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh and Ms Eileen Chong share our intent to reduce the stakes of our assessment milestones.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are not closed off to any ideas and will consult widely.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Over the years, many Members of Parliament (MPs), and most recently Mr Foo Cexiang at the Budget debate, have raised questions about why there is a need to set challenging questions at PSLE for secondary school selection.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Eileen Chong had also asked to remove the competitive grading element in PSLE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To address these questions, we must first consider what the role of PSLE is.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The PSLE serves as a checkpoint to assess students' understanding of core concepts and skills in the primary school curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It helps guide students into appropriate secondary school subjects and pathways that will best support their learning aspirations and needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To do this, we need a fair and consistent benchmark across all primary schools in Singapore and for students across all backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The PSLE today has a range of questions of varying difficulties, to help us identify students who might need more support with building up their foundations, as well as students who can benefit from further stretch in their next stage of learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For challenging questions, Members may like to know that students are provided with scaffolding support to help them apply the concepts and skills that they have learned in less familiar contexts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is a pen/pencil on the left side of your seat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: You may use your calculators on your mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will give you a few minutes to do page one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Look at page one and not page two, so that I can demonstrate to you what I have just said.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Page one shows two rectangular containers, X and Y.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the spirit of collaboration, you can consult your neighbours, across party lines is fine.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This problem assesses problem-solving skills, by testing how students apply mathematics in less familiar situations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In this case, the overflow of water, with real-world applications in future, such as engineering.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As you can see, this question is a bit more challenging.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will give you a few more minutes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Put your name and your seat number, and we will collect it later.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Part (a), if you look at it, is included to guide students to first find the volume of water in container X, which is the first step to solving the problem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Most students can solve part (a) and this is considered easy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Part (b) is more demanding, because when water was poured back from Y to X, some water overflowed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This assesses students' critical thinking to account for this change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But this is all based on the primary school syllabus and does not require knowledge beyond the syllabus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To help our students, challenging questions are often structured with scaffolding to help students attempt them progressively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On this note, we agree with Ms Eileen Chong that examinations, such as the PSLE, should not define students' self-worth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also agree with Ms Denise Phua and Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh that our schools should not just focus on academic results, and they indeed do not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because we recognise that ultimately, while grades might be the boat that gets you out to sea, it is resilience that keeps you afloat when storms hit; it is adaptability that helps you navigate changing currents; it is creativity that helps you spot new horizons; and it is interpersonal skills that will bring others with you in your journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And therefore, our schools seek to nurture students for life, and we broadly do it in two ways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members can continue working on the questions; we can cross-reference the answers later.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we place a lot of emphasis on holistic development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the primary, secondary and junior college levels, students develop 21st Century Competencies, such as adaptive and inventive thinking and civic literacy through the learning of subjects, Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) curriculum, CCAs and school-based programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our institutes of higher learning (IHLs) also build on schools' efforts by infusing life skills, such as interpersonal skills and innovation into curriculum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When I visit our schools, I like to ask our students what they dream of becoming when they grow up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some enjoy coding and say they want to work in IT or AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some are inspired by their teachers and want to become educators themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I also recall an enterprising student who told me that he dreams of starting his own business.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is good that our young ones are full of hope and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But our children also need to learn that for dreams to become reality, they need to take active steps and be resilient in dealing with challenges and setbacks along the way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also need to consider those who might not yet be sure about what they want to do when they grow up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are therefore aligned with Mr David Hoe and Mr Shawn Huang in providing our students exposure to the next stage of their school or work life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, some secondary schools offer Applied Learning Programmes (ALP) in areas, such as business and entrepreneurship, to connect classroom learning with real-world experiences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our polytechnic and ITE students are required to complete internships and can participate in career fairs, mentorship programmes and industry visits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These give our students exposure to different careers and industries to allow them to make more informed decisions on future pathways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, I have shared some of the moves we are exploring in Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we will study other countries and learn from their best practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Together, we will seek to create solutions that will ensure that our education system continues to meet our current and future needs, in particular with the changing and uncertain environment ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, we also want our schools to be active platforms that bring together students from different backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: After all, it is in our classrooms, school halls and sports arenas, where friendships are formed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And when students share their love of sports, music or mathematics, they discover that they are more similar than different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These interactions allow our students to bridge differences and develop social emotional skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our schools intentionally bring together students from different schools and different backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, we have combined school CCAs or cluster-based CCAs where students from different schools and backgrounds come together to learn and train on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This has ensured open access to all primary schools via Phase 2C.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, many of our schools have a good mix of students from families of different socio-economic statuses (SES).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nevertheless, there are still some schools that are overrepresented by students from higher-SES families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of these schools are located in neighbourhoods that comprise mostly private housing, with fewer public housing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the school is popular with parents, it might be filled first by those living nearest in private housing, because of the home-school distance priority.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Schools cannot just passively reflect the neighbourhoods around them, but they must also actively create diverse environments for our students to mix and mingle and to learn from one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have received many suggestions on the Primary 1 Registration Framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr David Hoe, Ms Lee Hui Ying and others have suggested removing the priority phases for children and siblings of alumni, including the affiliation advantage at Secondary 1 posting, as they feel that this is unfair and exclusionary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others have said the same of children whose parents volunteer for the school and community, because not every parent has the time and resources to do the same.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others support keeping things as they are, believing these connections help build school culture and shared values across generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On proximity, we have also heard equally diverse views.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some parents feel that proximity should be the most important consideration, so that students do not spend too much time traveling to and from school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others want to widen or even remove the home-school distance bands altogether, so that parents who can afford to buy or rent property near their preferred school do not get an unfair advantage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some have suggested that the same Primary 1 framework should not be rigidly applied to all schools, especially if the school's neighbourhood comprises mostly some types of housing over others.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And some have suggested that others from slightly further away be given some access.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For such schools, alumni priority could draw in diverse students from a wider geographical range, instead of only students from the nearby private estate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are all well-meaning suggestions and what I have just said is not exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we take every one of them seriously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But at the end of the day, we have to find the right balance between these competing views and needs, because there are only a finite number of places in each school and every change we contemplate would affect different groups in different ways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And as society evolves, we need to adjust this balance over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The rise of AI has changed the world as we knew it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: AI can increasingly accomplish more complex tasks and what once took us hours or days, AI can now accomplish in minutes or even seconds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, for all its capabilities, and they are growing, AI is not infallible, nor can it totally replace the humans' spirit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To prepare our workforce for an AI-transformed future, our schools and IHLs will equip our students to harness AI through the four "Learns".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Students will learn what AI is, how it works, what its impact is and what the limitations are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Students will learn how to harness AI tools effectively and responsibly, in partnership with the industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Educators will use AI in teaching and learning to enhance students' learning outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And fourth, perhaps the most important, learn beyond AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Educators will help students develop other critical skills, so that they can add human value and use AI to amplify their impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: My colleague, Minister of State Jasmin Lau will provide further details about MOE's AI-related moves and you must see them in the context of the overall national moves and national strategy on AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, since we started the SkillsFuture movement in 2015, training participation from both individuals and employers has significantly increased.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have provided significant financial support to empower individuals to take charge of their learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to strengthen accessibility of a larger range of courses for mid-career workers to upskill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: My colleague, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, will share more later.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we have done well, we can, must do more and do better, to support Singaporeans in navigating an increasingly complex economic landscape and one that is changing in an ever faster clip.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: My colleague, Minister Tan See Leng, will share more details at MOM's Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MOE will continue to steer the SkillsFuture movement together with MOM and the new agency and work with our IHLs, to provide high-quality, industry-relevant and accessible training for Singaporeans to upskill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The plans that I have outlined today cannot be achieved by MOE and our schools alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are grateful to our industry partners who closely collaborate with our IHLs to provide our learners with industry-relevant curriculum and real-world experiences that prepare our students for the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also appreciate our parent and school volunteers who plan engaging activities that strengthen student support and build stronger parent-child relationships.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in particular, I would like to recognise and affirm our educators for the important and hard work that they do day in, day out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To our school leaders and teachers, you are the core of our education system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: You nurture our students and support their learning – from lessons to remedials, from CCAs to camps, from building trust to journeying with students through difficulties and so much more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to ensure that our teachers are fairly recognised for their hard work and dedication.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also recognise that all the things you do for our students take time, effort and sacrifices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is therefore important that our teachers' workload remains manageable and sustainable and we have had extensive debates in this House before.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I have been sharing at length on our commitment in this front and we are making steady headway.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, by leveraging technology and AI, alongside the Reimagining the Teaching Profession Taskforce's recommendations, we will continue to help recalibrate what teachers do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include streamlining administrative processes, increasing support structures and protecting after-work hours, so that our teachers can better balance their professional responsibilities with their personal well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to listen to our teachers and do more to support you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chairman, I will now speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: (In Mandarin):   Colleagues, first, I want to wish everyone a Happy "Chap Goh Meh" and good health in the Year of Horse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The various initiatives that we are sharing today aim to support Singaporeans' learning needs and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Regardless of our student's starting point, we will ensure everyone has the opportunity to fulfil their potential, as we build a “we first” society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will do our best to cater to students with different strengths and needs, and uplift those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, all primary schools offer school-based programmes to develop and challenge students who have strengths and talents in English, mathematics and science.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will broaden access to existing school-based programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Students who can benefit from further stretch can choose to attend designated centres after school to participate in advanced modules.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This way, students can continue studying at their original primary school without having to transfer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These modules guide students to approach and solve real-life problems by making connections across different subjects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Whether students have strengths in a specific area or multiple areas, they can choose to participate in interdisciplinary modules during school holidays.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This year's Primary 3 students are the first cohort to participate in the refreshed identification process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will take a standardised test in August.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even if they are not selected the first time, students can still join the programme in Primary 4 and 5 if they are identified through other sources of information, such as teacher observations and their daily work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allows students to develop their strengths at their own pace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Education is an important driver of social equality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Regardless of their family background, our education system must give every child the opportunity to rise above their circumstances and achieve upward social mobility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From this year, we will devote more resources to support schools' after-school activities, providing mentoring, interest-based activities and learning journeys for students from low-income families to broaden their horizons and cultivate their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Schools will work closely with community stakeholders to provide more timely and comprehensive support for disadvantaged students and their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will strengthen coordination and collaboration between schools, Social Service Offices and Family Service Centres.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, we will increase special education school places and establish new schools to support more students with moderate to severe special educational needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Mr Chairman, this year, MOE's COS theme is "We Learn for Life Together".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: It reflects MOE's commitment to lifelong learning, which is salient given the rapid pace of change in technology in the world today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: But there is also another interpretation – which is apt given the many conversations we have had in this Chamber about AI – that we are nurturing our students to learn to live life the way life was supposed to be lived and to live together as friends, as a community, as one united people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: How do we want to nurture our students to live life?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We want to help our students find meaning, purpose and the motivation to pursue growth, so they can thrive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We want our students to not be defined by their pasts but have the courage to make the most of every situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We want our students to forge and build human connections with their friends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: How do we want to nurture our students to live together?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I think there is much for us to learn from our pioneers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We are all very familiar with the Singapore story.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Our forefathers of different races and religions had to learn to live together with each other.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: But our Pioneers overcame it, and Singapore flourished as a result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: And we need to build on their spirit and values.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We have heard much over this debate about how the world has changed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Against this backdrop, we need to nurture our students to be just as exceptional as our pioneers, if not more, and continue to have the same spirit and value of wanting to contribute to something bigger than ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: While the world builds walls, we must build bridges, starting in our classrooms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: When we prioritise our unity, harmony and stability, we create space for every student's holistic growth so that they can achieve their full potential, regardless of their starting point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Schools are one of the first places where children experience being in a community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Our schools offer shared experiences, which fosters our shared identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Our schools also offer the opportunity for students of different interests, talents and backgrounds to come together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Regardless of race, language or religion, we bring with us a diverse range of talents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Minister Desmond Lee spoke about plans to refresh, improve and broaden access to different modalities of support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: This includes refreshed support for primary school students with strengths in the academic domain, as well as expansion of the SPED school capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Beyond that, students who need more academic support also receive targeted intervention in schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Support programmes are delivered in small groups using customised resources and are taught by specially trained teachers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Students have flexibility to customise their learning of individual subjects in their secondary school journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: They do so based on their individual strengths, interests and learning needs instead of keeping to a single subject level for all subjects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: At the lower secondary levels, students are placed in mixed form classes to interact with classmates of different profiles and strengths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: They spend about a third of their curriculum time in their mixed form classes and learn together for subjects such as art, physical education, design and technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: The Full SBB pilot has shown encouraging outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Students are forming friendships and they display more positive attitudes towards peers from different backgrounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: They also have a stronger sense of belonging to their schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Teachers also observe students taking greater ownership of their own learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Students demonstrate stronger motivation to overcome challenges and break through limiting mindsets to pursue subjects at more demanding levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: He started at one of the Full SBB pilot schools, St Andrew's School, entering through Posting Group 1.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: He was originally disheartened because none of his friends were in the same posting group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: But under Full SBB, Samuel's starting point did not define him or how he would finish.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: He was offered the opportunity to take English, mathematics and sciences at G2 level at Secondary 1, and he had the flexibility to continue his other subjects at G1 level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Even as he juggled a more demanding academic load alongside rugby training, Samuel remained consistent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: When he felt ready, he took on all subjects at G3, the most academically demanding subject level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: With Full SBB, Samuel could learn at his own pace, and he could take ownership of his learning journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: He was not defined by labels, but he carved out his own path, on his own terms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: With the right support system, every student can achieve their full potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Samuel did well for his GCE "O" Level in 2025 and is now pursuing his studies at Temasek Polytechnic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: The first Full SBB cohort will be sitting for the SEC examination in 2027.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Today, GCE "N" and "O" Level graduates have to navigate multiple admissions processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: There are different application portals and timelines for various educational pathways, such as the Joint Admissions Exercise (JAE), Polytechnic Foundation Programme (PFP) Admissions Exercise and Institute of Technical Education Joint Intake Exercise (ITE JIE).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: As a result, students need to keep track of different application processes and timelines, which may create more uncertainty regarding their posting choices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: All pathways and courses are available for selection on a single platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Students can see all the courses that they are eligible for, and they can select and rank their choices based on their preference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Students will no longer need to keep track of various admissions exercises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Tie-breakers will be applied when two students with the same net aggregate score are vying for the last available vacancy in the course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We hope that this more student-centric approach will allow all our students to reach their full potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Beyond enabling students to reach their full potential based on their unique strengths, Full SBB has also created opportunities for students to foster meaningful connections.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Adam from Bendemeer Secondary School took subjects across G1 to G3 levels which gave him more opportunities to make friends from different classes.
